query: For high-entropy alloys intended as intermediate materials in plasma-facing reactor components, what single intervention could improve heat-transfer capability while preserving structural integrity? Formulate one hypothesis specifying the intervention, its mechanism, the expected outcome compared with current intermediate-layer performance, the temperature and loading conditions under which it should hold, supporting prior evidence, and a controlled experiment that would falsify the hypothesis.

generation.hypothesis: Introducing a minor amount of cobalt (~5 at%) into a tungsten‐rich refractory high-entropy alloy intended for use as the intermediate thermal barrier will enhance its heat-transfer capability by promoting higher-frequency phonon and electron transport, while the low doping level preserves the BCC phase and microstructural stability required for structural integrity under reactor conditions.
generation.material_initial_state: A tungsten-based refractory HEA (e.g., a (CrFeTiTa)70W30-type alloy) currently used as an intermediate thermal barrier layer between tungsten and CuCrZr components in fusion reactor designs.
generation.intervention: Chemically modify the alloy by substituting a minor fraction (~5 at%) of one of the constituent elements with cobalt.
generation.conditions: The intervention is intended to be effective under the high heat flux, elevated temperatures (approximately 600–1000 °C), and irradiation environments typical of plasma-facing reactor components.
generation.structural_mediator: Retention of the single-phase BCC structure with minimal changes in grain-boundary precipitates that ensure both high-temperature strength and irradiation resistance.
generation.mechanism: Co is known to promote high-frequency phonon vibrations and can enhance electronic contributions to heat conduction. Its introduction in small amounts is expected to reduce alloy disorder scattering that otherwise limits lattice thermal conductivity, thereby increasing overall thermal transport while keeping the phase stability and mechanical strength intact.
generation.predicted_outcome: The Co-doped HEA is expected to show a measurable increase (on the order of roughly 10–20% enhancement) in effective thermal conductivity relative to the undoped baseline, with unchanged or potentially even improved high-temperature strength and ductility.
generation.baseline: The performance metrics (thermal conductivity, strength, and microstructural stability) of the undoped tungsten-rich HEA used as the intermediate layer.
generation.boundary: This beneficial effect is anticipated only with low levels of Co doping; higher Co concentrations may destabilize the BCC structure or introduce excessive solute segregation, thereby harming mechanical properties and irradiation resistance.
generation.uncertainty: Precise quantitative improvement in thermal conductivity is uncertain and depends on the optimal Co concentration and interaction with other elements. This hypothesis builds on the observed effects of elemental tuning in CoCrFeNiCu alloys (PMC11369437) and the high-temperature stability of tungsten-based HEAs (PMC11901246) while extending these results to fusion-relevant conditions, which remain to be verified.

falsification_experiment.design: Fabricate two sets of the tungsten-rich HEA intermediate layers—one set with ~5 at% Co doping and one undoped control. Subject both to thermal cycling at 600–1000 °C combined with simulated irradiation conditions representative of plasma-facing environments. Evaluate thermal transport and mechanical integrity before and after exposure.
measurements: Thermal conductivity using transient thermoreflectance or similar methods
High-temperature mechanical properties (tensile/compressive strength and ductility)
Phase stability and microstructure analysis via XRD and SEM
falsification_experiment.falsification_rule: If the Co-doped alloy fails to demonstrate at least a 10% improvement in thermal conductivity without any degradation (or with a significant degradation) in mechanical properties and microstructural stability compared to the undoped sample, the hypothesis is falsified.

cited_evidence.text: AbstractHigh entropy alloys (HEAs) are alloys composed of five or more primary elements in equal or nearly equal proportions of atoms. In the present study, the thermophysical properties of the CoCrFeNiCu high entropy alloy (HEA) were investigated by a molecular dynamics (MD) method at nanoscale. The effects of the content of individual elements on lattice thermal conductivity kp were revealed, and the results suggested that adjusting the atomic content can be a way to control the lattice thermal conductivity of HEAs. The effects of temperature on kp were investigated quantitively, and a power-law relationship of kp with T−0.419 was suggested, which agrees with previous findings. The effects of temperature and the content of individual elements on volumetric specific heat capacity Cv were also studied: as the temperature increases, the Cv of all HEAs slightly decreases and then increases. The effects of atomic content on Cv varied with the comprising elements. AbstractNuclear fusion is a promising energy source. The International Thermonuclear Experimental Reactor aims to study the feasibility of tokamak-type reactors and test technologies and materials for commercial use. One major challenge is developing materials for the reactor’s divertor, which supports high thermal flux. Tungsten was chosen as the plasma-facing material, while a CuCrZr alloy will be used in the cooling pipes. However, the gradient between the working temperatures of these materials requires the use of a thermal barrier interlayer between them. To this end, refractory high-entropy (CrFeTiTa)70W30 and VFeTiTaW alloys were prepared by mechanical alloying and sintering, and their thermal and irradiation resistance was evaluated. Both alloys showed phase growth after annealing at 1100 °C for 8 days, being more pronounced for higher temperatures (1300 °C and 1500 °C). The VFeTiTaW alloy presented greater phase growth, suggesting lower microstructural stability, however, no new phases were formed. Refractory multiprincipal element alloys (rMPEAs) are potential materials for the plasma-facing components in future fusion reactors due to their high melting point, strength and irradiation resistance. However, the concurrent optimization of ductility and high-temperature properties remains a significant challenge due to the complex interdependence between alloy chemistry, mechanical behavior, and thermodynamic stability.
